anchors.paper_title: MNE-BIDS: Organizing electrophysiological data into the BIDS format and facilitating their analysis
anchors.paper_venue: The Journal of Open Source Software
anchors.reason: MNE-BIDS is a software tool paper for organizing data into BIDS; the dataset README says it was generated with MNE-BIDS, so it is not a paper about this dataset.

anchors.paper_title: EEG-BIDS, an extension to the brain imaging data structure for electroencephalography
anchors.reason: EEG-BIDS is a data-organization standard extension used to format this dataset, not a paper describing this alphabetic decision task dataset.

metadata.methods_description: EEG data were recorded during an alphabetic decision task and converted to BIDS format using MNE-BIDS, combined with behavioural data, stimulus information, and metadata. Known data issues (e.g., restarted recordings, channel swaps, interrupted sessions) were documented and corrected during BIDS conversion. Recording timestamps were anonymised by a constant time shift.

citation_details.title: Beyond Letters: Optimal Transport as a Model for Sub-Letter Orthographic Processing
citation_details.author: Jack Edward Taylor, Rasmus Sinn, Cosimo Iaia, Christian J. Fiebach
citation_details.abstract: Letter processing plays a key role in visual word recognition. However, word recognition models typically overlook or greatly simplify early perceptual processes of letter recognition. We suggest that optimal transport theory may provide a computational framework for describing letter shape processing. We use representational similarity analysis to show that optimal transport cost (Wasserstein distance) between pairs of letters aligns with neural activity elicited by visually presented letters <225 ms after stimulus onset, outperforming an existing approach based on shape overlap. We additionally show that optimal transport can capture the emergence of geometric invariances (e.g., to position or size) observed in letter perception. Finally, we demonstrate that Wasserstein distance predicts neural activity similarly well to features from artificial networks trained to classify images and letters. However, whereas representations in artificial neural networks emerge in a computationally unconstrained manner, our proposal provides a computationally explicit route to modeling the earliest orthographic processes.
